title: I wept too much
hook: Seneca admits he grieved his friend Annaeus Serenus beyond measure (Letters 63)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ictus animi, the jolt even the wise feel. Your line was the first jolt.

Lucilius has lost a friend named Flaccus, and he's taking it hard. Seneca writes back with the advice a Stoic is supposed to give: grieve, but within measure. Don't let your eyes stay dry, and don't let them flood. Weep, but don't wail. It's sensible and balanced. Then, near the end of the sixty-third letter, Seneca does something unexpected in a letter of advice. He turns the light on himself, and tells his friend about the time he didn't follow his own advice at all.
screen: `LUCILIUS LOSES FLACCUS.` → `WEEP, BUT DON'T WAIL.` → `THEN SENECA TURNS THE LIGHT ON HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Seneca's rule for grief sits in the middle: let the eyes be neither dry nor overflowing. Tears are natural. Endless, performed grief, he thinks, often has more to do with being seen to grieve than with the friend. Then the confession. I write this to you, he says, I who wept for my dear friend Annaeus Serenus so far beyond measure that, against my will, I'm one of the examples of people conquered by grief. Serenus was younger than Seneca, and a close friend. Seneca had never once considered that Serenus might die first. He'd thought only of their ages, as if death went in order. Now, he says, I condemn myself for that, because I didn't think it could happen. A teacher who'd never failed his own rule would be easier to admire and harder to trust. Seneca gives Lucilius the rule and the stumble together, and the stumble makes the rule human. Looking back on the week, from the dark house to the seasick swim to the tunnel, the man keeps telling stories against himself. The lesson isn't don't weep. It's: weep, and don't pretend it couldn't happen.
screen: `NEITHER DRY NOR OVERFLOWING.` · `I WEPT FOR SERENUS BEYOND MEASURE.` · `I NEVER THOUGHT HE'D GO FIRST.` · `THE STUMBLE MAKES THE RULE HUMAN.` · then, large: `GRIEF IS HONEST.`

segments.voice: Go gently here; if a loss is very fresh, simply breathe and rest instead. Otherwise, bring to mind one person or thing you've lost and let yourself feel whatever is there, sadness, anger, numbness, even relief, without measuring it. If tears come, let them; if not, that's fine too, and breathe with the loss as you'd sit with a friend.
Lacrimae. Latin for tears: Seneca confesses he wept for his friend Serenus far beyond his own rule that grief stay neither dry nor overflowing. Today's word.
Your line: grief is honest. Honest even when it overflows. Another week of letters, done.

howItsDone: Readers of Seneca often take from this letter permission to grieve honestly, and to admit when grief has overflowed their own expectations.
